blocks.text: Organic nitrogen compounds are essential to life and to the modern world. Amino acids and nucleotides, the basis of proteins and nucleic acids, contain nitrogen. Amines and nitro compounds are important in the dye industry and in medicines; nylon, Kevlar and polyurethane are nitrogen-containing polymers; and nitrogen compounds are also found in food, fertilisers and explosives.

blocks.title: Interesting information: caffeine and theobromine
blocks.text: Caffeine in coffee and theobromine in chocolate are both organic nitrogen compounds; they are active compounds that make our mood happy. What is the difference between these two?

blocks.alt: Two displayed structures side by side, each a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring with labelled C and N atoms, two C=O groups and N-CH3 groups. Caffeine has CH3 on three ring nitrogens; theobromine has H instead of CH3 on the left-hand nitrogen.
blocks.caption: Caffeine and theobromine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 119).

blocks.text: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogen atoms of NH3 are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. The number of hydrogen atoms replaced is the basis of their classification. In IUPAC nomenclature amines are called alkanamines.

items: Primary amines: one alkyl or aryl group on the -NH2 group, e.g. methanamine CH3NH2, ethanamine CH3CH2NH2, propan-1-amine CH3CH2CH2NH2 and phenylamine (aniline) C6H5NH2.

blocks.alt: Primary amines: CH3-NH2 labelled methanamine, CH3-CH2-NH2 labelled ethanamine, CH3-CH2-CH2-NH2 labelled propan-1-amine, and a benzene ring with NH2 labelled phenyl amine (aniline).
blocks.caption: Primary amines: methanamine, ethanamine, propan-1-amine and phenyl amine (aniline) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 119).

items: Secondary amines: two groups on an -NH- group, e.g. N-methylmethanamine CH3NHCH3, N-methylethanamine CH3NHCH2CH3 and diphenylamine (C6H5)2NH.

blocks.alt: Secondary amines: CH3-NH-CH3 labelled N-methylmethanamine, CH3-NH-CH2-CH3 labelled N-methylethanamine, and two benzene rings joined through NH labelled diphenyl amine.
blocks.caption: Secondary amines: N-methylmethanamine, N-methylethanamine and diphenyl amine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 119).

items: Tertiary amines: three groups on the same nitrogen atom, e.g. N,N-dimethylmethanamine (CH3)3N and triphenylamine (C6H5)3N.

blocks.alt: Tertiary amines: N,N-dimethylmethanamine drawn with three CH3 groups on N (one above, one either side), and triphenylamine, an N atom joined to three benzene rings.
blocks.caption: Tertiary amines: N,N-dimethylmethanamine and triphenylamine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 119).

items: Quaternary ammonium salts: tetra-substituted nitrogen, e.g. tetramethylammonium chloride [(CH3)4N]+ Cl-.

blocks.alt: Tetramethylammonium chloride: a nitrogen atom with four CH3 groups (above, below, left and right) inside square brackets with a + charge outside the bracket, followed by Cl-.
blocks.caption: Tetramethylammonium chloride, a quaternary ammonium salt (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 120).

blocks.title: Branching at nitrogen
blocks.text: Whether an amine is primary, secondary or tertiary depends on the branching at the nitrogen atom, not at the carbon attached to it. This is not the same as for alcohols or halogenoalkanes.

items: Draw (write) structures for 2,4-dimethylhexan-3-amine, N-methylpentan-1-amine, 2-methylcyclohexan-1-amine and N,N-dimethylethanamine.
